Instructor Teaching Plan: Meeting #27 (Lesson 10.2 — Receiving a Pull Request)

Date: Friday, November 13, 2026 Time: 9:30 – 10:20 AM (50 mins) Room: MULH 3032 Context: Week 10 (Consolidation) · Meeting 2 of 2 Milestone: Pull request reviewed and merged; conflict resolved; validation sweep clean
PEDAGOGICAL ENTRY STATE AUDIT:
On Tuesday (10.1) the class met the git vocabulary and connected repositories to GitHub as origin. The session ran short: it ended at the moment Ace received a pull request notification. Nobody has yet reviewed or merged a pull request, brought a merge back to the laptop, or resolved a merge conflict. Expect the vocabulary to be half-remembered; the recap on slide 4 is there to fix that, not to reteach it.
OPERATIONAL TARGET & CORE DIRECTIVE:
Using Ace's waiting pull request as the live example, walk through the owner's four steps (read, review, decide, merge) and the routine that follows every merge (checkout main, fetch origin, merge origin/main, log). Then every student makes and resolves a conflict in their own repository and runs xmllint --noout on every TEI file, so that most of the Module 10 assignment is finished before they leave.

Before Class (5 minutes)

  • Confirm Ace's pull request is still open and note whether GitHub reports conflicts; if it has been merged or closed, open a one-line pull request on a teaching repository to use instead.
  • Ask Ace beforehand whether she is willing to drive on the projector; if not, drive from her repository yourself with her permission.
  • Have the manuscript image for the changed line open in a second tab.

Walk-in Music (plays as students arrive, before minute 0)

  • Kraftwerk, “Autobahn” (1974, Philips / Vertigo). Built on a steady, repeating machine rhythm.
  • Pedagogical connection: Git collaboration is a small set of moves repeated the same way every time. A pull request is a car at the on-ramp: it joins main only when the owner lets it in.
  • Springboard at minute 0: “On Tuesday Ace got a pull request. Nothing in her edition has changed yet. Today we learn what the owner does next.”

THE OBJECTIVE: THE PULL REQUEST AS AN EDITORIAL DECISION

A pull request is a proposal, not a change. Main changes only at the merge, and only after someone has read the changed lines against the manuscript image. When two readings collide, Git refuses to guess and hands the decision back to the editor, who resolves it from evidence and records the choice in a commit.

INVIOLABLE PEDAGOGICAL BOUNDARIES

1. Review against the image: Every changed reading in Files changed is checked against the facsimile, not memory.
2. Fixes go on the same branch: An author answers review comments with add, commit and push on the existing branch, never a second pull request.
3. Bring every merge home: After any merge on GitHub, run checkout main, fetch, merge and log before starting new work.
4. No leftover markers: A resolved file contains no conflict markers and passes xmllint --noout.
5. Module 10 assignment deadline: Due tonight, Friday, November 13, at 11:00 PM: merge commit hash, validation output, and a 100–150 word note in CONSOLIDATION.md.

Review (slide 6): in Files changed, read one red/green pair against the image; leave one inline comment and one suggestion.
Decide (slide 7): Review changes → Approve (or Request changes, if the reading is wrong; then show the author pushing a fix to the same branch).
